newsitem.title: USA: Lebanon looks to U.S. to help Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon looks to U.S. to help Mideast peace.

text.p: Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri said on Friday the Middle East peace process had "almost stopped" and appealed to the United States to help jump-start it.

"You know, the peace process is almost stopped. We hope that soon the United States will be ready to do anything needed to help the peace process," Hariri said while attending a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new Boston University building he helped to fund.
Hariri, who is expected to meet with President Bill Clinton later on Friday, said prospects for peace in the region depended on Israel.
"It's up to the Israelis to decide now if they want to go ahead with the peace process or not," said the prime minister.

Since the latest round of Middle East peace talks were launched in 1991, Syrian and Lebanese accords with the Jewish state have been linked and Hariri said they would stay that way because Lebanon did not want to be left out of a deal.
Syria is the dominant foreign power in Lebanon, with 35,000 Syrian troops in the country, and its peace with Israel has long been considered central to regional peace.
Hariri, who met with Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Thursday, will ask Clinton to accede to Lebanon's request for arms and to lift a U.S. travel ban on the country.
Hariri has said his government was looking to Washington for helicopters, armoured personnel carriers, communications equipment and aircraft.
The United States, which saw a series of its citizens kidnapped by Islamic fundamentalist groups in Lebanon in the 1980s, insists the travel ban is purely for security reasons.

But Lebanese officials say their country is now much safer than many countries Americans are not barred from visiting. They allege the ban is politically motivated to force Lebanon into a peace agreement with Israel.
Hariri said he would tell Clinton: "The country is safe. Everybody is coming and going with no problems. Security is very high, I assure you."
Lebanon's southern region is still occupied by Israeli troops, with the Islamic fundamentalist group Hizbollah actively resisting what Hariri has called an "occupation."
